The hardest changes (cross-cutting design, gnarly concurrency, subtle algorithms) go to your strongest judgment model (`claude-opus-5-5-xhigh`), whether the task needs judgment on vague intent or is a precisely specified sequence of steps to execute to the letter. Trivial mechanical edits go to your fast code model. Per-role lines in the `/setup-pstack` rule override these defaults and the model choices in the routed skills (`how`, `why`, `arena`, `swarm`, `architect`, `interrogate`, `reflect`). A role with no line keeps its default, and a role line of `inherit-parent` or `auto` runs that role on the parent chat model (omit Task `model`). Prose and judgment read `judgment and prose`.

edits.old: **Match the model to the job.** Before each spawn, start from the role's line or default and pick the reasoning level and speed the job needs. The `/setup-pstack` budget sets each role's starting level, xhigh by default. Raise it one step, up to max, for the hardest or subtlest work. Lower it one step for judgment and two or more steps for routine work. Use fast mode only when the job is urgent, meaning CI or trunk is red or a person is blocked on the result right now. Otherwise use standard speed, the same slug without `-fast`. Verification is the exception and stays on the `swarm workers` model and speed (`grok-4.7-xhigh-fast` by default). Change only the effort level and whether the slug is fast, and keep the family the role names, so a diverse panel stays diverse. If the family has no slug at that level and speed, use its nearest slug. A role on `auto` or `inherit-parent` stays on the parent model. If the Task tool rejects the adjusted slug, do not try another adjusted slug. Use the role's line or default and say so. If the Task tool rejects that too, continue with the calling skill's fallback. A slug counts as rejected once a Task error says that the model is not valid, or leaves the slug out of its list of valid slugs. Never pass a rejected slug, and skip any fallback whose slug is already rejected. When the calling skill has no fallback, use the closest valid slug of the role's family from the error's list of valid slugs, or omit `model` so the subagent runs on the parent model when the list has none. When the calling skill's fallback runs out of slugs without saying what to do next, omit `model` too. Say so in both cases.

Never translate a slug, omit a rejected selector, or substitute a family default. Native preflight remains authoritative. Report actual attribution. Repeated parent selections are samples, not a diverse panel.

edits.old: **Verification.** Tests alone are not sufficient verification. A PR is verified only when its unit, live, and perf boxes are all checked (the **prove-it-works** principle skill). That sentence is the verification rule. Every verification block opens with it. The live block is mandatory. Ten lanes at the PR head drive the real surface through its control skill, per the **swarm** skill, on the `swarm workers` model (default `grok-4.7-xhigh-fast`). Each lane is one box with a concrete scenario, the screenshot it saves, and its pass predicate. One lane is the **Regression lane against trunk.** It runs the same load-bearing scenario on trunk and head. If trunk does not have the feature, the lane records that fact and gates the behavior the diff adds plus the end state the user waits for instead of inventing a trunk result. The perf gate is dual-sided. Trunk and head must both produce the named metric. If trunk lacks the feature, also isolate the work the diff adds and set an absolute budget for that work plus the end-to-end state the user waits for. Do not claim a ratio between unlike scenarios. The perf block names the metric, the interleaved probe, the trunk baseline measured first, and the rule with the number that fails. A PR that changes an interaction is review-gated. The operator reviews it in chat with screenshots and a video before merge. A PR that changes no interaction writes `**Review gate.** None. <PR id> is not review-gated.` and no boxes under it.

edits.old:
Whether `/poteto-mode` stays on depends on how the user starts it:

- Enter on `/poteto-mode` attaches the skill to one message. It fades as the chat moves on.
- Option+Enter on Mac or Alt+Enter on Windows, or Use as Mode from the skill entry, makes it a Custom Mode. It stays in context every turn until the user exits the mode, and it stays out of casual turns.
- Cursor's docs list Custom Modes in the Agents Window and the CLI. Elsewhere, start each new task with `/poteto-mode`.

Link [Cursor's skills docs](https://cursor.com/docs/skills) when this comes up. Mid-chat, "new task" makes the mode match a fresh playbook. `/poteto-mode` already uses `poteto-agent` for the subagents its playbook steps spawn. To get the same style from a subagent of your own, spawn it with `subagent_type: "poteto-agent"`.
edits.new: Bare `/poteto-mode` enables branch-local persistent mode without inference. `/poteto-mode off` and `/skill:poteto-mode off` disable it. Use `/skill:poteto-mode <task>` for task-bearing activation. There is no Custom Mode gesture. Short task-bearing commands are unsupported in one-shot modes. Role data applies independently of mode.

1. Use the **create-skill** skill (Cursor's built-in for authoring SKILL.md files).
2. Validate the skill: frontmatter has `name` and `description`, referenced files exist, cross-skill links resolve.
3. Test cases if structural. Skip if subjective.

edits.new:
1. Choose the scope before writing. Use `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` in the project or `~/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` for a personal skill. Preserve an existing Pi-discovered destination. Never edit package caches or generated package resources. Show the destination and honor the calling workflow's approval gate.
2. Write YAML frontmatter with `name` and `description`. Use a lowercase hyphenated name matching the directory, at most 64 characters. Keep the description a single YAML scalar, at most 1024 characters, stating what the skill does and when to use it. Use `disable-model-invocation: true` for explicit-only skills.
3. Write direct, ordered instructions with concrete inputs, commands, expected results, failure handling, and retained evidence paths. Keep supporting files beside the skill and link them relative to its directory. Apply the **unslop** skill. Do not invent unavailable tools or weaken mandatory gates.
4. Validate frontmatter, referenced files, and cross-skill links. Run `/reload` in Pi from the project, inspect discovery warnings, and invoke `/skill:name` with a representative task. Resolve name collisions before claiming the intended skill loaded.
5. For structural workflows, run a positive case and a negative or missing-capability case. Retain actual tool results and fix failures before repeating. For description tuning, try matching and non-matching prompts and inspect whether the skill was loaded. Lexical checks are not model-compliance evidence. Subjective mode prose needs the user's review rather than a fabricated benchmark. Report unrun cases as limitations.
6. Follow the calling workflow's delivery and approval rules. Run **Opening a PR** only when authorized. Reflect's no-push rule still applies.

edits.old: Create `.cursor/skills/verify-<app>/features/README.md` plus one file per user-facing feature you can identify (aim for the top 3-5 to start, from routes, commands, menus, or docs). Follow the shape in [`references/feature-map-example/`](references/feature-map-example/), with a README index and one file per feature. Each file answers, from the user's point of view: what the feature is, how to reach it, how to drive it with the harness, and what observable end state proves it works. The four H2s are `Sub-features`, `How to get to it (user POV)`, `Driving it with <harness>`, and `Gotchas`. If the seed data lacks a precondition that a journey needs, the journey reports a failure and the reason goes in that feature's `Gotchas`. Never weaken the journey to make it pass. The map is the repo's maintained verification source; a proof that drives one convenient entry point is incomplete when the map lists others.

edits.new: Use the Pi adapter's session acquisition procedure before reading history. Scope reads to the current Pi session or exact authorized retained session paths supplied by the operator or a retained native run record. Cross-chat mining without an authorized corpus is blocked. Never search a sessions tree or use Cursor transcripts as a fallback. Pi JSONL starts with a session header and contains typed entries, not just chat messages.

edits.old: 3. Fan out across your chat history. Spawn parallel subagents on a fast, cheap model, each taking a slice of the corpus. Tell every subagent to order candidates by real modification time (`ls -t`) and never by UUID name, grep the topic first and then read only the matching chats and only their relevant regions, and skip the current chat plus obvious noise (subagent, eval, and test chats). Each returns the same schema, one block per chat: topic, the user's goal, decisions, open threads, struggles and corrections, and artifacts (PRs, tickets, branches), each citing the chat UUID. For one or two chats, skip the fan-out and search directly. The raw transcripts stay in the subagents. The main thread gets only their findings. Pick each subagent's reasoning level and fast or standard speed for the job, per the Subagents section of the **poteto-mode** skill.
edits.new: 3. Search only the authorized corpus. For one or two sessions, read directly. Otherwise partition the exact authorized paths among native subagents. Filter by the agreed time window and topic, then read relevant entries. Each finding cites the exact path and entry ID, with the topic, goal, decisions, open threads, corrections, and artifacts. Do not skip the current session when it is the only authorized evidence. Label a current-session-only brief as incomplete for cross-chat recall. Follow native role data for any delegated review.
